 57% of Employers Are Offering Higher Salaries for Skilled Talent. At 63, Her New Job Can Replace a Low-Earning Year and Raise Her Social Security
 A new job at 63 can do something most workers never realize: permanently raise a Social Security check for the rest of your life. But whether that actually happens depends entirely on what is already sitting in your earnings record.
 By Gerelyn Terzo 
 Published November 5, 2026, 2:03pm ET · 4 min read 
 The Full Benefits Desk desk. Editor: Gerelyn Terzo .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 Social Security bases your benefit on your highest 35 years of earnings, and any new year that beats your lowest year permanently raises your check.
 An $85,000 job replacing a zero year raises Carol's monthly benefit by about $65, but replacing a $50,000 year yields only $27 more.
 Claiming early while working can trigger withholding of $1 for every $2 earned above $24,480, but that reduction reverses at full retirement age.

 A recent salary survey found 57% of hiring managers are offering more pay than they planned to land skilled workers. For Carol, a hypothetical 63-year-old project manager who stepped away from work for several years to raise kids and later care for a parent, that reality hits differently. A better-paying job now could pad her savings, and it could also raise her Social Security check for the rest of her life.
 She has plenty of company in wondering how late-career work shows up in a benefit. Even someone still working at 78 can see a higher Social Security check if new earnings replace zeros or other low-earning years in the calculation.
 Your Benefit Rests on 35 Years, and Weak Years Can Be Swapped Out
 Social Security bases your benefit on your highest 35 years of earned income on which you paid Social Security taxes. Earnings before age 60 are adjusted up for wage growth across the economy, while earnings paid for work done after age 60 are not indexed and count at face value. If you worked fewer than 35 years, zeros fill the gaps.
 Every new year of work gets compared against the lowest year in your top 35. If the new year is bigger, it bumps the lowest one out and your average rises. If you are already collecting, Social Security reviews your record each year and, when the new year makes the cut, recalculates your benefit and retroactively pays you any increase .
 That average then runs through a formula. The percentages are 90%, 32% and 15%, with the dollar thresholds set in the year you turn 62. For Carol, who turned 62 in 2025, the thresholds are $1,226 and $7,391. Many middle earners fall in the 32% band, where each additional dollar of average monthly earnings adds 32 cents to their full retirement benefit.
 Which Year Gets Bumped Matters More Than the Size of the Raise
 Say Carol’s new job pays $85,000. Social Security spreads the additional earnings across the 420 months in 35 years. Assuming the increase falls in the 32% bracket, here’s how the salary affects her monthly benefit at full retirement age (FRA):
 If it replaces a zero year from her caregiving stretch, her check rises by about $65 a month, or roughly $780 a year, for life.
 If it replaces a year worth $50,000 after indexing, the gain drops to about $27 a month, or around $324 a year.
 If her lowest year in the top 35 already tops $85,000 after indexing, her benefit stays exactly where it is. The raise still helps her paycheck and retirement savings.
 A smaller raise at a job that eliminates a zero can do more for her check than a bigger one that only replaces a decent year. Whatever increase she earns also compounds with future cost-of-living adjustments , and the 2027 adjustment is 3.6%.
 Collecting Early While Working Brings a Separate, Temporary Rule
 Carol was born after 1960, so she reaches retirement age at 67. If she had already claimed at 62, the earnings test would apply. In 2026, Social Security holds back $1 for every $2 earned above $24,480. On an $85,000 salary, that works out to $30,260 withheld over the year, enough to erase most of a typical check.
 One worker considering a new job paying $12,500 a month asked whether their benefit would drop to zero. For a stretch, it could. Once Carol reaches FRA at 67, Social Security recalculates her benefit to credit the months it withheld payments. The earnings limit is higher in the year she reaches 67 and disappears starting that month.
 These two effects run on different clocks. Withholding is a temporary cash-flow squeeze. Replacing a lowest year is a permanent raise.
 Check Your Earnings Record Before Counting on a Bigger Check
 The most useful step costs nothing: log into your online account, pull your earnings history, and find the lowest years in your top 35. Zeros or very low years mean a well-paid job at 63 can raise your check. A record full of strong years means the new salary mostly helps your savings. Either way, compare the offer, your planned retirement date, and an updated benefit estimate side by side before assuming the raise changes anything.
 If you haven’t claimed yet and the new job pays well above the earnings-test limit, holding off on claiming keeps the withholding from eating your check, and every month of waiting raises the benefit too. Your claiming date is much harder to undo than a job change, so make that call with your actual record in front of you. Two people with the same salary offer can end up with very different answers, and the details of your own history decide which one you get.
